newsitem.title: TURKEY: Unrepentant Turk Islamists hope for early polls.
newsitem.headline: Unrepentant Turk Islamists hope for early polls.

text.p: Turkey's Islamists remain as committed as ever to increasing the role of religion in public life despite a mauling from the secularist establishment that forced them out of power.

Analysts say former prime minister Necmettin Erbakan, never wholly comfortable with the restrictions of office, will push his Islamist agenda harder now he is in opposition, and prove a thorn in the flesh of successor Mesut Yilmaz.

"It's in the nature of them to go for the maximalist position and the rhetoric. I see them hardening in opposition," said a Western diplomat with close contacts in Erbakan's Islam-based Welfare Party.
But the Islamist dream of returning to government with enough MPs to rule without needing secularist coalition partners is distant.

Erbakan, 70, will shrug off a recent wave of anti-Islamist criticism from the army and media in the hope he can win the next round in what he sees as a struggle for the heart and soul of modern Turkey that could take years to unfold.
"They will not change their spots. To give them their dues, they are the only Turkish party that really believes in something and has a long-term view," the diplomat said.
Yilmaz is expected to defeat the Islamists and their conservative allies at a confidence vote on July 12.
His left-right alliance of three parties has begun to waver on a promise to hold early elections next spring now that it is settling into office.
Most observers see elections, initially due by the year 2000, being called in mid-1998 or later that year.
"The rag-tag government is frightened of going to the nation," Welfare's daily paper Milli Gazete said on Wednesday. "They cannot escape elections," it predicted.

Erbakan is bitter at the manner in which the secularists, led by President Suleyman Demirel, closed ranks to keep him out of office after he resigned last month in a bungled attempt to hand over power to conservative coalition partner Tansu Ciller.
"Demirel will not be able to live this down for the rest of his life. It is a deceitful use of force against parliament," Erbakan told a defiant meeting of his MPs on Tuesday.
However, Erbakan's resignation is not as great a loss to the Islamists as it may seem.
He had attempted to go to early polls himself in a test of strength with the military and the new government will only delay ballotting by about six months beyond the date the Islamists had planned.

Army pressure ensured that Erbakan was getting nowhere with mild Islamist plans such as lifting a ban on women civil servants wearing headscarves and erecting mosques in traditional secularist areas of Ankara and Istanbul.
He left office just as the generals, who toppled three previous governments since 1960, began making noises about a fourth military intervention. Voters were also uneasy.
"Society needed breathing space," said commentator Mehmet Ali Birand. "People were fed up with fights and Welfare saw that," he said.
Erbakan is still believed to be one of the country's most popular politicians, although opinion polls are notoriously inaccurate.

Observers say the Islamists' claims to 40 percent of the vote are exaggerated but that Welfare's support among the disaffected urban poor should not be underestimated. The party won 21 percent at the last general elections, in 1995, and squeezed into power thanks to secularist disunity.
"Quite a few people, including those who wish them ill, fear they will go up to between 25 and 30 percent," the diplomat said.
"They will probably go up a couple of percentage points," said Birand. He predicted an attempt to have Welfare banned by the constitutional court for alleged Islamist extremism could backfire.
"There could only be an explosion of support if they close down the party or try to throw Erbakan in jail," he said.
A sizeable Islamist election victory would test the army's avowed commitment to democracy and willingness to defy a warning from staunch NATO ally Washington not to use force.

"The military, after having the experience of the last year, don't want it to happen again. But short of an overt coup they can't completely fly in the face of what the next elections may bring," the diplomat said.
